title: Suez Reopening: What It Means for Europe's Ports | Flexport
summary: Carriers are returning to Suez, shortening transit times but risking port congestion in Europe. See what to expect and how to prepare your cargo.
body_markdown:
---


Article


Carriers are announcing Suez returns at a faster pace. As of October 21, Alphaliner reports that 63% of Far East-Europe capacity is back on the Suez in at least one direction, and every top-five carrier now sends at least some ships through the canal.


## Good news for shippers: more space and shorter lead times


Diversions around the Cape of Good Hope tied up about 6% of global container capacity. Each service that returns to Suez frees ships and saves 7-10 days of transit to the first Mediterranean port, 10-14 days to North Europe and 10-14 to US East Coast ports.


## The bad news: Europe's ports could jam first


When Suez transits stopped initially, there was broad port congestion as vessels were out of position and bunching up – we’re likely to see the same effect as transits resume. Flexport data shows 129% of normal capacity arriving in North Europe starting in week 45 (November 2 to 8). As more services return, ships will bunch at key European ports and hubs. Rotterdam yards already run 80% to 90% full, and barge and rail handling runs 36 to 48 hours behind. The upcoming holiday period and with recent strikes, will put the yard utilization and berthing schedules under pressure.


And as containers arrive early, warehouses will not all be ready and trucking and rail capacity will be short. Plan for port delays even when the ocean leg gets shorter.


## The open question: where does the freed capacity go?


For the major head-haul trades, the Transpacific pays far more. Mid-October SCFI had Asia to the US East Coast at $10,524/FEU vs. $3,556/FEU to Europe. Carriers could move ships to the Transpacific, which would ease space and rates there. Or maybe they’ll send them elsewhere, with SCFI to South America at $6,031/FEU for the same period. Carriers are currently reviewing their networks, and it’s clear that if Suez sees a full return, the capacity freed up will help ease the current constraints.


## Your cargo may arrive before you’re ready for it


Containers that arrive early still have to be collected. Cargo left at the terminal accrues storage, demurrage and detention charges, and it keeps yards full, which slows discharge for everyone and makes the congestion worse. Hapag-Lloyd’s CEO has said that customers’ ability to pull boxes out of the yards worries him more than the ships bunching.


## What to do now:


1. Decide which cargo must stay off Suez, and ask your insurance broker whether war-risk cover still applies if a carrier re-routes mid-voyage. Some insurers don’t offer Suez cover, if that applies to your business, reach out to your Flexport representative, as we can consider it in our planning of your cargo.
2. As not all routings go through Suez, make sure you consider the shipment level estimated delivery dates for warehouse planning vs a standard lead time. The situation continues to evolve and our platform is updated to give you the latest information on shipment level.
3. Update delivery dates and warehouse slots for earlier arrivals in Europe for impacted shipments and routes.
4. Build extra buffer for port and inland delays in North Europe from week 45.
5. Confirm you can receive cargo on arrival. Check warehouse space, dock appointments, trucking and drayage, and have a plan for early or off-dock storage if you can’t take it in.


## The route can still reverse


The Houthis now hold Yemen’s entire Red Sea coast, including islands in the Bab el-Mandeb strait. They say general shipping may pass, Saudi-linked vessels excepted, but that can change from one day to the next. Drewry estimates the Suez saving at about $1 million per round voyage for the largest ships, and a 0.3% war-risk premium on a $225 million ship wipes it out. Evergreen and ZIM still avoid the route. A reversal would re-tighten the trade within one sailing cycle, so confirm routing and war-risk cover on each sailing.


Continue to monitor the flow of ships at[atlas.flexport.com](https://atlas.flexport.com/) .


Sources: Alphaliner (Oct 21, 2026); Linerlytica via Seatrade (Sep 1, 2026); Flexport Ocean Market Update (Sep 2026); Flexport Suez wave data.
